narrativeReportMd:
# SubstanceSpecification R4-to-R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
Breaking changes were found. R6 ballot4 does not define a same-named `SubstanceSpecification` resource; the local successor is `SubstanceDefinition`, and the successor model remodels several high-value local backbones.

## Scope
This report compares the R4 `SubstanceSpecification` StructureDefinition with the R6 `SubstanceDefinition` successor found in the local R6 core package. Inherited `Resource`/`DomainResource`/`Element` changes are excluded from findings and listed as out of scope.

## Main migration themes
The migration requires a first-class cross-version transform, not a text replacement. After resource identity is changed, implementers must handle remodeled `property` and `relationship` backbones, removed specialized companion-resource references, source/representation document changes, molecular-weight cardinality tightening, local terminology tightening, and modifier semantics on `status`.

## Highest-impact findings
The highest impact findings are the artifact identity break, property remodeling, relationship remodeling, and removal or folding of specialized companion references. These can make R4-valid instances fail R6 validation or lose data unless manually transformed.

## Findings requiring human review
Human review is especially important where no official mapping was available: property strings and defining substances, relationship Range amounts, source-material and specialized companion-resource data, isotope details, and language terminology mappings.

## Backward-compatible design observations
Several changes appear semantically motivated, but a deprecated alias, official maps, or transitional optional fields would have reduced migration risk. Optional R6 additions are forward-compatible but create significant R6-to-R4 round-trip loss.

## Follow-up analysis
Base artifact changes, companion substance resources, terminology expansions, and official ballot narrative/change notes should be reviewed separately before implementing production transforms.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: `SubstanceSpecification` has material local breaking changes from R4 to the R6 ballot: the same-named resource is gone and the probable successor is `SubstanceDefinition`. The biggest migration concerns are the root resource rename, remodeled property/relationship/source-material content, and loss or restructuring of specialized companion-resource references. Confidence is high for structural deltas from local packages, but official mapping and terminology expansions would improve migration guidance.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Migration is not a simple resourceType rename. Implementers need a version-aware transform that first maps `SubstanceSpecification` to `SubstanceDefinition`, then rewrites local children with changed names and content models. The highest-risk areas are substance properties, relationships, specialized companion references, source/representation documents, molecular weight/isotope data, and status/name-language conformance semantics. R6-to-R4 conversion is lossy unless extensions or companion-resource mappings are defined for R6-only content.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high that the same-named R6 artifact is absent and that `SubstanceDefinition` is the successor candidate because this is directly supported by package indexes, the R6 StructureDefinition, and the R6 `fhir-old-types` code system. Confidence is lower for some semantic mappings because no official diff, StructureMap, ConceptMap, narrative migration guide, or terminology expansions were available.

findings.title: SubstanceSpecification is not present as an R6 resource; the probable successor is SubstanceDefinition

oldState.summary: R4 defines a concrete resource named SubstanceSpecification.

semanticText.definition: The detailed description of a substance, typically at a level beyond what is used for prescribing.

oldState.narrativeMd: The R4 package contains `StructureDefinition-SubstanceSpecification.json` with `type` and `id` both equal to `SubstanceSpecification`, `kind` = `resource`, and `abstract` = `false`.

newState.summary: The same-named R6 StructureDefinition is absent; R6 defines SubstanceDefinition instead.

semanticText.definition: The detailed description of a substance, typically at a level beyond what is used for prescribing.

newState.narrativeMd: The assigned R6 path is absent. The R6 package index contains `StructureDefinition-SubstanceDefinition.json`, and the R6 `fhir-old-types` code system lists `SubstanceSpecification` as an old resource name no longer used in this version.

facts.note: R6 marks this as an old resource name no longer used.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: `SubstanceDefinition` is the only R6 `StructureDefinition-*Substance*.json` resource that carries the same high-level description as R4 `SubstanceSpecification`. The R6 package also explicitly lists `SubstanceSpecification` in `fhir-old-types`. No official ConceptMap or narrative diff was available, so element-level mappings are still assessed as migrations rather than guaranteed aliases.

impact.impactRationaleMd: A conforming R6 validator or parser will not accept `resourceType: "SubstanceSpecification"` as an R6 resource type. Code generated from the R6 package will expose `SubstanceDefinition`, not `SubstanceSpecification`, so REST routing, profile URLs, canonical references, switch statements, and generated model classes all need an explicit cross-version mapping. In the reverse direction, an R6 `SubstanceDefinition` instance is not an R4 `SubstanceSpecification` instance without changing `resourceType`, canonical URLs, references, and renamed elements.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Substance definition data can affect medicinal product, ingredient, and regulatory workflows. A missed resource rename can lead to rejected exchanges or unprocessed substance records.

justification.inferredGoal: Rename and remodel the detailed substance artifact around a definition-oriented resource name.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep the R6 base resource named `SubstanceSpecification` while clarifying its definition and preferred terminology, or retain a deprecated same-named base alias.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The goal of positioning the artifact as a substance definition is reasonable, but the identity break is not clearly necessary. The computable evidence shows the R4 resource name disappeared and `SubstanceDefinition` is the successor, yet the same domain goal could largely have been met by retaining the R4 resource identity and improving definitions, mappings, and conformance text.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: The best less-breaking base design would have kept `SubstanceSpecification` as the R6 resource type and canonical StructureDefinition while updating the description and internal model to reflect definition-oriented semantics. If HL7 wanted to introduce `SubstanceDefinition`, retaining `SubstanceSpecification` as a deprecated base alias would also reduce parser, routing, and reference breakage, though that alias approach risks two canonical names for the same concept.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Avoids the root resourceType break at the cost of living with a less precise legacy name; an alias would add duplicate canonical resource names.

evidence.detail: R6 package index contains `SubstanceDefinition` but no `SubstanceSpecification`.
R6 `SubstanceDefinition` has the same high-level description as the R4 assigned resource.
evidence.quote: The detailed description of a substance, typically at a level beyond what is used for prescribing.

evidence.detail: R6 marks `SubstanceSpecification` as an old FHIR type no longer used.
evidence.quote: An old resource name no longer used in this version of FHIR (deleted or renamed).

examples.examplesMd: The fragments illustrate the identity break only; real migrations must also transform element names, references, and content models.

findings.narrativeMd: The largest break is at artifact identity. R6 does not ship a `SubstanceSpecification` StructureDefinition at the assigned path; instead, the comparable substance-detail resource is `SubstanceDefinition`. Existing R4 data, code, canonical URLs, and references that name `SubstanceSpecification` need an explicit migration step before any element-level comparison matters.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An R4 instance with `resourceType: "SubstanceSpecification"` can be valid in R4 and fail R6 validation solely because the resource type is not defined. Conversely, an R6 `SubstanceDefinition` instance is not R4-representable as-is. This affects strict JSON/XML parsers, generated model libraries, REST endpoint dispatch, FHIRPath expressions rooted at the old type, and reference target validation.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Introduce a first-class cross-version mapping from `SubstanceSpecification` to `SubstanceDefinition`. Update resourceType values, canonical profile URLs, reference targets, generated class names, persistence discriminators, route names, and tests. Do not treat this as a simple prefix rename: several local elements also changed shape and require separate transforms.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The package evidence suggests a deliberate rename or replacement. A backward-compatible alias or official map would have reduced breakage, but it would also preserve an obsolete resource name in the R6 core model. Without such an alias, clients must implement a version-aware transformation.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: The successor match is strong but inferred from local package evidence rather than from an official diff or ConceptMap.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R6 ballot4 does not define a same-named `SubstanceSpecification`; the local successor evidence points to `SubstanceDefinition`. That is a real resource identity break for `resourceType`, REST routes, generated classes, canonical URLs, and references. I do not treat the rename as automatically disproportionate because the R4 resource was FMM 0/trial-use and current IDMP-oriented public material points at `SubstanceDefinition`, not continued use of the R4 name. The break still needs explicit migration rules, but the base-design direction looks defensible.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition-SubstanceSpecification has id/type/url `SubstanceSpecification` and R4 maturity map lists FMM 0, trial-use.
R6 package has StructureDefinition-SubstanceDefinition and no StructureDefinition-SubstanceSpecification at the assigned path.
R6 CodeSystem-fhir-old-types includes `SubstanceSpecification` as an old resource name no longer used.

HL7 R5/R6 SubstanceDefinition pages describe the same detailed substance-definition role; UMC IDMP API IG says GSIDs are manifested through `SubstanceDefinition` and documents a production FHIR server.
freshReview.fmmEffect: R4 FMM 0/trial-use substantially softens the stability expectation. The substance domain is regulatory and implementation-relevant, but the quick public check found current use centered on `SubstanceDefinition`, not evidence that the R4 `SubstanceSpecification` name must be preserved.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid plus runtime/API/codegen: an R4 instance, endpoint, profile, or generated model named `SubstanceSpecification` is not accepted as R6 `SubstanceDefinition` without a transform.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: R6 could have kept the old resource name or added a deprecated alias, but that would preserve a FMM0 legacy canonical and likely create duplicate resource identities for the successor model. The alternative is real, but not clearly low-cost enough to make the rename itself a design problem.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing high-impact finding because the identity break is real; disagree with treating the less-breaking alternative as a straightforward Yes, since aliasing a core resource type has substantial long-term cost.

findings.title: Property backbone was remodeled: optional code became mandatory type, string values and defining substance details were removed

oldState.summary: R4 property entries had optional `code`, optional `category`, optional `parameters`, optional `definingSubstance[x]`, and `amount[x]` as Quantity or string.
oldState.narrativeMd: In R4, a `property` item could be valid with only `amountString`, only `parameters`, or a `definingSubstanceReference`/`definingSubstanceCodeableConcept`; `property.code` was optional.

newState.summary: R6 property entries require `type` and use `value[x]` with CodeableConcept, Quantity, Range, date, boolean, or Attachment; the R4 category, parameters, and definingSubstance fields are absent.
newState.narrativeMd: In R6, every `property` repetition has `property.type` with cardinality `1..1`. The value is carried in `property.value[x]`; there is no `valueString`, and the separate defining-substance and parameter fields are not present.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The parent element name stayed `property`, but the children changed substantially. `property.code` is the closest semantic match for R6 `property.type`; R4 `property.amount[x]` is the closest source for R6 `property.value[x]`.

impact.impactRationaleMd: After mapping the resource identity, an R4 `property` entry that lacks `property.code` cannot satisfy R6 `property.type` `1..1`. An R4 `property.amountString` has no direct R6 `property.valueString` representation. R4 `category`, `parameters`, and `definingSubstance[x]` are unknown R6 elements and must be discarded, transformed into other fields, or preserved with extensions. In the reverse direction, R6 property values of type CodeableConcept, Range, date, boolean, or Attachment are not direct R4 `amount[x]` values except where a semantic down-map is defined.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Loss or misclassification of substance property data can affect regulatory interpretation, matching, and analytical property workflows.

justification.inferredGoal: Generalize property values and make the property type explicit for each repetition.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain deprecated R4 property children while adding `type` and generalized `value[x]`, with required typing enforced by profiles or warnings during transition.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The R6 goal appears reasonable: make each property typed and generalize value representations. A fully compatible base design would not cleanly meet that goal because R4 allowed untyped properties and used several old child elements with different semantics. The remaining less-breaking options are transitional and materially increase ambiguity.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: R6 could have preserved `property.code`, `amount[x]`, `category`, `parameters`, and `definingSubstance[x]` as deprecated fields while adding `property.type` and `property.value[x]`. That would preserve many R4 instances, including old quantity/string values, but it would create overlapping same-resource representations for the same fact and would not guarantee that all properties have a meaningful type unless stricter profiles rejected some legacy records.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Improves compatibility but leaves duplicate property encodings, weaker base validation for untyped properties, and long-term implementation burden.

evidence.detail: R6 `property.value[x]` allows CodeableConcept, Quantity, Range, date, boolean, or Attachment, but not string.
R4 allowed a defining substance as Reference(SubstanceSpecification|Substance) or CodeableConcept; no same child exists in R6.

examples.examplesMd: The migration example is illustrative. A real transform needs domain rules to decide whether a legacy string is a coded value, free text extension, or rejected data.

findings.narrativeMd: The `property` backbone is not a simple rename. R6 requires a typed property and changes the value slot. Old R4 instances that treated `code` as optional or used `amountString`, `parameters`, or `definingSubstance[x]` need active remediation rather than mechanical field renaming.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An R4-valid `property` with no `code` can become R6-invalid because `property.type` is required. An R4 `amountString` has no R6 choice element, so strict validators will reject it after a naive transform. R6 values using new choices such as boolean or Attachment cannot round-trip to R4 `amount[x]` without loss or extensions.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Map `property.code` to `property.type` when present. Inventory property entries missing `code`, and define a fallback policy before migration. Map Quantity values directly to `valueQuantity`; avoid automatic mapping of strings unless a domain-specific representation is approved. Preserve removed `category`, `parameters`, and `definingSubstance[x]` with extensions or manual curation where they carry business meaning.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change improves regularity but was only partly backward-compatible. Adding the new `value[x]` and `type` while retaining old fields would have allowed gradual migration, at the cost of duplicate representations and weaker validation.

freshReview.narrativeMd: The `property` backbone changed in ways that can reject or lose central substance-characterization data: R4 allowed an untyped property, string amounts, measurement parameters, and a defining substance; R6 requires `property.type` and drops those old children while using a different `value[x]` set. This is not just a code cleanup. Migration may require expert judgment to decide whether text, parameters, or defining-substance context becomes a coded value, another relationship, or preserved legacy content.
keyEvidence: R4 `SubstanceSpecification.property.code` is 0..1 and `property.amount[x]` is Quantity|string.
R4 `property.category`, `property.parameters`, and `property.definingSubstance[x]` are local children.
R6 `SubstanceDefinition.property.type` is 1..1 and `property.value[x]` is CodeableConcept|Quantity|Range|date|boolean|Attachment, with no string choice.
R6 concise element extraction found no direct `category`, `parameters`, or `definingSubstance[x]` child under `SubstanceDefinition.property`.
freshReview.fmmEffect: R4 FMM 0/trial-use prevents assuming broad deployed impact from the break alone, but `property` is a core substance-description path and the loss can affect regulatory or analytical interpretation, so low FMM does not neutralize the concern.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: R4 properties missing `code`, using `amountString`, or carrying removed child elements are not valid R6 `SubstanceDefinition.property` content after a mechanical rename.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: A less-breaking base design could have added `valueString` back to R6 `property.value[x]` and retained `parameters` or `definingSubstance[x]` as deprecated optional children while encouraging the new typed model. Making `type` mandatory has a clearer computability goal, but the string/context removals look like modest-cost compatibility points. The tradeoff is duplicate property encodings and weaker guarantees that every property is fully normalized.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree that affected instances can hard-break; disagree with the existing Probably justified framing because some compatibility-preserving choices, especially retaining string/context carriers, seem plausible enough to warrant review.

findings.title: Relationship backbone now requires a relationship type and narrows amount/reference details

oldState.summary: R4 relationship had optional `relationship`, optional `substance[x]`, `amount[x]` including Range, `amountRatioLowLimit`, and `amountType`.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 allowed a relationship repetition without a relationship code. It could use `amountRange`, and a reference target named `SubstanceSpecification`.

newState.summary: R6 relationship uses mandatory `type`, renamed `substanceDefinition[x]`, `amount[x]` without Range, `ratioHighLimitAmount`, and `comparator`.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 requires `relationship.type` `1..1`, targets `SubstanceDefinition` for references, removes Range from `amount[x]`, and renames the amount qualifier fields.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: Names and definitions make the mapping clear: R4 `relationship.relationship` corresponds to R6 `relationship.type`, and R4 `relationship.substance[x]` corresponds to R6 `relationship.substanceDefinition[x]`.

impact.impactRationaleMd: A relationship entry that was valid in R4 without `relationship.relationship` cannot satisfy the R6 mandatory `type`. R4 `amountRange` has no R6 choice. References must retarget from `SubstanceSpecification` to `SubstanceDefinition`, so reference validators and generated code need a migration rule. Reverse conversion has similar naming issues but can usually map `type` back to `relationship` if no R6-only semantics are used.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Substance relationships such as active moiety, salt-to-parent, starting material, and impurity relationships can be clinically or regulatorily meaningful. Dropping the type or amount semantics can change interpretation.

justification.inferredGoal: Make the relationship type explicit and align references with the renamed resource.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep the old optional `relationship.relationship` and Range amount as deprecated alternatives while adding the R6 `type` and renamed fields.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Requiring an interpretable relationship type and aligning references with the successor substance resource are reasonable R6 goals. Less-breaking choices exist, especially retaining the old name and `Range` choice, but they would preserve incomplete or ambiguous relationship records in the base model.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A transitional base design could have kept `relationship.relationship` optional as an alias for `type`, retained `amountRange`, and made required typing a profile rule or warning. That would reduce immediate invalidation of R4 data but would leave consumers handling two names for relationship type, more amount forms, and untyped relationships that R6 appears to be trying to avoid.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves more R4 records but weakens the base guarantee that relationships are typed and leaves duplicate amount/name representations.

evidence.detail: R4 relationship code is optional `0..1 CodeableConcept`.
R6 relationship type is mandatory `1..1 CodeableConcept`.
R6 relationship amount allows Quantity, Ratio, or string, but not Range.

examples.examplesMd: The example shows both risk mechanisms: a missing mandatory type and an R4 Range amount that has no direct R6 choice.

findings.narrativeMd: The relationship backbone became more explicit but less permissive. The old optional `relationship` field is now mandatory as `type`, the target resource is renamed, and `Range` is no longer an allowed amount representation. Implementers cannot safely migrate relationship arrays without checking each repetition.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Old relationship entries missing a type are R4-valid but R6-invalid. Old `amountRange` values fail type validation in R6. Existing references to `SubstanceSpecification/{id}` need target rewriting or they will fail reference target checks in R6 profiles and generated clients.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Map `relationship.relationship` to `relationship.type`; flag missing values for curation. Convert `substanceReference` targets from `SubstanceSpecification` to `SubstanceDefinition`. Decide whether Range amounts should become a Ratio, string, high-limit field, or extension. Include tests for relationships missing type, using Range, and referencing another substance resource.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The stronger R6 model is defensible, but a deprecated alias plus warning-level invariant would have allowed data migration without immediately invalidating incomplete R4 records.

freshReview.narrativeMd: `relationship` became stricter and narrower: the relationship code is now required as `type`, the referenced resource target follows the resource rename, `Range` is removed from `amount[x]`, and amount qualifier names changed. A relationship such as salt-to-parent, active moiety, impurity, or starting material can be substance-identity relevant; dropping a range or requiring a missing type is not safely mechanical for all records.
keyEvidence: R4 `SubstanceSpecification.relationship.relationship` is 0..1 CodeableConcept.
R6 `SubstanceDefinition.relationship.type` is 1..1 CodeableConcept.
R4 `relationship.amount[x]` includes Quantity|Range|Ratio|string; R6 includes Quantity|Ratio|string and omits Range.
R4 `relationship.substance[x]` references SubstanceSpecification; R6 `relationship.substanceDefinition[x]` references SubstanceDefinition.
freshReview.fmmEffect: The R4 FMM 0/trial-use status softens the presumption of deployed compatibility, but this path is central to substance relationships and can be regulatory or safety relevant, so the lossy/expert-dependent cases still justify renewed attention.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: R4 relationship repetitions without a relationship code or with `amountRange` fail the R6 content model unless curated or transformed.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: R6 could have retained `Range` in `relationship.amount[x]` and kept the old `relationship` child as a deprecated alias or transitional optional element while encouraging `type`. Keeping `type` required improves computability, but preserving Range seems a relatively low-cost widening. The tradeoff is duplicate names and weaker enforcement of typed relationships.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the hard-break assessment; disagree with the existing conclusion that the break is simply probably justified, because the Range removal and mandatory-type transition appear to have plausible less-breaking base alternatives.

findings.title: Specialized R4 substance companion references were removed or folded into the new model

oldState.summary: R4 linked out to specialized resources for reference information, nucleic acids, polymers, proteins, and source material.
oldState.narrativeMd: The R4 `SubstanceSpecification` resource had local elements that referenced several R4-only substance resources. Those companion resources were present in the R4 package index.

newState.summary: R6 has no same-named StructureDefinitions for those companion resources; only an inline `sourceMaterial` backbone remains on SubstanceDefinition.
newState.narrativeMd: The R6 package contains `SubstanceDefinition` and `Substance`, but not `SubstanceReferenceInformation`, `SubstanceNucleicAcid`, `SubstancePolymer`, `SubstanceProtein`, or `SubstanceSourceMaterial` StructureDefinitions. `sourceMaterial` is now an inline backbone with limited taxonomic/anatomical fields.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The source-material concept is retained by name but changes from a reference to an inline backbone. The other specialized references have no direct R6 `SubstanceDefinition` child with the same names in the local package.

impact.impactRationaleMd: Any R4 `SubstanceSpecification` instance that carries these reference elements will contain unknown elements after an identity-only migration to R6. The referenced R4 resource types also are not available in the R6 package, so bundles containing those resources need a higher-level consolidation strategy. R6 inline `sourceMaterial` content cannot be represented in R4 `SubstanceSpecification.sourceMaterial` without creating or referencing an R4 `SubstanceSourceMaterial` resource or using extensions.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Protein, polymer, nucleic acid, and source-material details are key substance characterization data. Lossy migration may alter regulatory substance identity.

justification.inferredGoal: Consolidate the substance-specific companion resources into a simplified R6 substance definition model.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Retain the specialized companion reference elements and their target resource types as deprecated R6 content while introducing the simplified inline model.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Consolidating the substance model is a plausible R6 design goal, and retaining all R4 companion targets would materially undermine that simplification. The break remains high-risk because referenced protein, polymer, nucleic-acid, reference-information, and source-material payloads can be important and no official map was available in the local inputs.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design would have kept `referenceInformation`, `nucleicAcid`, `polymer`, `protein`, and reference-style `sourceMaterial` as deprecated optional elements, with the old companion StructureDefinitions still valid as R6 targets. That is a real base-design alternative, not merely migration tooling, but it carries major long-term costs: implementers would need to support both the old specialized resource family and the newer simplified inline representation.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Protects legacy substance detail but keeps a broad old companion-resource family in core and duplicates simplified R6 representations.

evidence.detail: R4 references specialized nucleic acid, polymer, and protein resources.
R6 package has no `StructureDefinition-SubstanceReferenceInformation`, `-SubstanceNucleicAcid`, `-SubstancePolymer`, `-SubstanceProtein`, or `-SubstanceSourceMaterial` entry.

examples.examplesMd: The examples focus on structure shape. Companion resource payloads require their own analysis and are not expanded in this SubstanceSpecification report.

findings.narrativeMd: R4 `SubstanceSpecification` depended on a family of specialized companion substance resources. R6 `SubstanceDefinition` no longer exposes those reference elements, and the package does not contain those companion StructureDefinitions. This is a local break for `SubstanceSpecification` because the local elements disappear or change from reference to inline content.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 instances with `referenceInformation`, `nucleicAcid`, `polymer`, `protein`, or reference-style `sourceMaterial` will not validate against R6 `SubstanceDefinition` without transformation. Bundles containing the referenced resources also need conversion; otherwise references dangle or target unknown R6 resource types.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Inventory all uses of the companion references. For `sourceMaterial`, map only fields that have an R6 inline equivalent and preserve the rest with extensions or curated annotations. For nucleic acid, protein, polymer, and reference-information payloads, wait for or define domain-specific mappings before discarding data. Test bundle-level referential integrity, not just individual resources.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The R6 simplification may be justified if the companion resources were considered too granular, but removing reference targets without published maps is highly disruptive. Deprecated targets or standard extensions would have enabled less lossy migration.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R4 `SubstanceSpecification` could point to a family of specialized substance resources for reference information, nucleic acids, polymers, proteins, and source material. R6 removes those target resource types from the local package and only retains `sourceMaterial` as a smaller inline backbone. This can orphan bundle content or force lossy consolidation of high-value substance details, and no local official map was available to show a safe replacement.
keyEvidence: R4 local elements reference SubstanceReferenceInformation, SubstanceNucleicAcid, SubstancePolymer, SubstanceProtein, and SubstanceSourceMaterial.
R6 package index search found no StructureDefinition entries for those specialized companion resources.
R6 `SubstanceDefinition.sourceMaterial` is an inline BackboneElement with type, genus, species, part, and countryOfOrigin children.
UMC IDMP API IG shows substance identifiers are current implementation content, reinforcing regulatory relevance, but it uses `SubstanceDefinition` rather than the old R4 companion family.
freshReview.fmmEffect: Low R4 FMM reduces the expectation that the old companion-resource family must remain stable, but the affected data can be central to regulatory substance identity. The possible loss of whole referenced payloads outweighs the low-FMM softening for this finding.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid with R6-to-R4 loss: old reference elements become unknown in R6, old target resource types are absent, and R6 inline source-material data cannot be represented as the old R4 reference without creating another resource or preserving data elsewhere.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: A less-breaking R6 base design could have retained the specialized reference elements and companion StructureDefinitions as deprecated optional content while introducing the simplified inline model. That is costly because it keeps a broad legacy model alive, but the amount and importance of potentially lost data make the tradeoff worth standards review.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the existing high-impact assessment and partial-alternative framing; strengthen the action judgment to Revisit because the migration is payload-level, lossy, and not resolved by local evidence.

findings.title: Structure representation changed from inline Attachment to DocumentReference, and source was renamed

oldState.summary: R4 allowed an inline `Attachment` for structural representation and used `structure.source` for supporting literature.
oldState.narrativeMd: An R4 structural representation could carry an embedded attachment directly under `structure.representation.attachment`; structure-level sources were in `structure.source`.

newState.summary: R6 uses `structure.representation.document` as a Reference(DocumentReference), adds `format`, and renames `structure.source` to `structure.sourceDocument`.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 separates the representation string, representation format, and a document reference. Inline attachment bytes are not accepted directly in the representation backbone.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The R6 `document` definition describes an attached file with the structural representation, which matches the role of the R4 `attachment` element, but the representation type changes from inline data to a resource reference.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 instances carrying `structure.representation.attachment` become invalid because R6 has no such element, and the nearest replacement expects a `Reference(DocumentReference)`, not an `Attachment`. A lossless migration may need to create contained or external DocumentReference resources. Reverse conversion can inline a DocumentReference attachment only if the referenced document is available and semantically suitable.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Chemical structure representations can be key identity evidence. Losing a MOLFILE, SDF, image, or analytical document can affect downstream matching or review.

justification.inferredGoal: Normalize structural representation files as document references and distinguish logical representation format.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Allow both the old inline `Attachment` and the new `Reference(DocumentReference)` representation during a transition.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Normalizing structural files through `DocumentReference` and adding an explicit format element is a coherent R6 goal. A less-breaking choice could preserve inline attachments, but it would leave two competing ways to carry the same structural artifact and make consumers handle both inline and referenced document lifecycles.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: R6 could have retained `structure.representation.attachment` or made the document-bearing element a choice that accepted either `Attachment` or `Reference(DocumentReference)`. That would preserve R4 instances with embedded MOLFILE, image, or other data, but it would dilute the normalized document model and complicate provenance, access control, and retrieval behavior.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves inline payloads but creates duplicate retrieval/provenance patterns for structural representation files.

evidence.detail: R6 adds a CodeableConcept format element.

examples.examplesMd: The contained DocumentReference example is one possible pattern; implementations may instead store the document externally.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 changes how structural files are carried. Inline attachments under the representation backbone must become references to DocumentReference resources, and source references are renamed. This is a serialization and persistence concern for systems that store molecular files in the resource itself.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: A valid R4 resource with `structure.representation.attachment` is invalid in R6 because the element is removed. A naive transform to `document` will still fail unless it creates a Reference. Reverse conversion depends on resolving the referenced DocumentReference and choosing whether to inline its attachment.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: During R4-to-R6 conversion, create contained or external DocumentReference resources for inline attachments, copy attachment metadata, and set `structure.representation.document`. Map `structure.source` to `structure.sourceDocument`. Add tests for inline data, URL-only attachments, and missing referenced documents.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The new model is cleaner for document management, but allowing an Attachment-or-Reference choice would have preserved old instances. The tradeoff is inconsistent retrieval and duplicate ways to represent the same artifact.

freshReview.narrativeMd: The structural representation file carrier changes from an inline `Attachment` to a `Reference(DocumentReference)`, and `structure.source` is renamed to `sourceDocument`. This is a real serialization and persistence break for resources that embed structure files, but the R6 design has a coherent document-management goal: representation files can carry provenance, lifecycle, access, and retrieval behavior through DocumentReference.
keyEvidence: R4 `structure.representation.attachment` is 0..1 Attachment.
R6 `structure.representation.document` is 0..1 Reference(DocumentReference).
R6 adds `structure.representation.format` as CodeableConcept.
R4 `structure.source` and R6 `structure.sourceDocument` both target DocumentReference.
freshReview.fmmEffect: R4 FMM 0/trial-use softens stability pressure. The path can matter for molecular identity evidence, but the change is narrow and usually migratable by creating contained or external DocumentReference resources.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: an inline R4 Attachment is not the R6 element shape; a transform must create or reference a DocumentReference.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: R6 could have allowed an Attachment-or-Reference choice or retained `attachment` as deprecated. That would preserve old instances, but it would duplicate retrieval and provenance patterns and weaken the normalization benefit of using DocumentReference.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree with the existing assessment that this is a medium, real break with a partial less-breaking alternative whose tradeoffs make the R6 change probably acceptable.

findings.title: Molecular weight now requires an amount and isotope-specific structure was removed

oldState.summary: R4 molecular weight reused the isotope molecularWeight backbone; `amount` was optional, and isotope-specific details existed under `structure.isotope`.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 `SubstanceSpecification.molecularWeight` and `structure.molecularWeight` were content references to `structure.isotope.molecularWeight`; the nested `amount` field was `0..1`. R4 also had a repeatable `structure.isotope` backbone with identifier, name, substitution, halfLife, and isotope molecular weight.

newState.summary: R6 defines an explicit molecularWeight backbone whose `amount` is mandatory `1..1`; `structure.isotope` is absent.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 `SubstanceDefinition.molecularWeight.amount` is `1..1 Quantity`. `structure.molecularWeight` content-references the new top-level molecularWeight. The R4 isotope subtree is not present.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The shared `molecularWeight` name and content-reference definitions identify the migration path. The R6 top-level molecular weight is stricter because the quantitative amount is required.

impact.impactRationaleMd: R4 allowed molecular weight entries that had only method or type, because amount was optional in the referenced backbone. R6 requires `amount`, so those entries become invalid. R4 isotope-specific fields have no direct R6 location in `SubstanceDefinition`, creating data-loss risk for isotope-rich substance records.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Molecular weight and isotope data can be part of substance identity and analytical characterization. Missing or moved values may affect matching or regulatory review.

justification.inferredGoal: Make molecular weight entries quantitatively meaningful by requiring an amount and simplifying the isotope model.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep molecular-weight `amount` optional with a warning/profile requirement and retain isotope details as a deprecated optional backbone.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Making molecular-weight entries quantitatively meaningful is reasonable, but the combined break is not fully justified by the local evidence. Requiring `amount` rejects historical records that carried method or type only, and removing isotope-specific content has no clear replacement in the supplied StructureDefinitions.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: A less-breaking base design could have left `molecularWeight.amount` optional while adding a best-practice warning or profile requirement for complete records, and could have retained `structure.isotope` as deprecated content. This would not fully satisfy a strict base guarantee that every molecular weight has an amount, and it would preserve additional legacy complexity, so the alternative is only partial.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves incomplete and isotope-rich R4 records but weakens base validation and keeps extra legacy structure.

evidence.detail: R4 top-level molecularWeight content-references the isotope molecularWeight backbone.
R4 has a repeatable isotope backbone.

examples.examplesMd: The migration example intentionally shows that inventing an amount is unsafe; production migration should not use dummy quantities without policy approval.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 makes molecular weight more concrete by requiring an amount, but that creates a hard validation issue for R4 records that only supplied method or type. Separately, the R4 isotope backbone disappeared from `SubstanceDefinition`, so isotope-related substance characterization needs a different representation.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: An R4 molecularWeight entry with children but no `amount` can satisfy R4 `ele-1` but fail R6 cardinality. R4 isotope data fails because `structure.isotope` is unknown in R6. R6 molecularWeight values can usually be represented in R4, but not if R6 semantics rely on the simplified top-level model without an agreed back-map.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Before migration, find molecularWeight entries missing `amount` and decide whether to derive, curate, or omit them. Do not insert arbitrary quantities solely to pass validation. Preserve isotope details with extensions or domain-specific resources if required. Test both top-level and structure-level molecularWeight content references.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Requiring an amount is semantically cleaner but could have been introduced as a profile or warning first. Removing isotope-specific fields is harder to assess without official rationale or replacement guidance.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R6 makes molecular-weight `amount` mandatory and removes the R4 isotope subtree. Requiring an amount is sensible for complete molecular-weight data, but R4 allowed method/type-only molecular-weight entries, and isotope details such as identifier, substitution, half-life, and isotope molecular weight have no direct R6 location in the checked StructureDefinition. That combination can force invented quantities or loss of isotope-specific substance characterization.
keyEvidence: R4 top-level and structure-level `molecularWeight` content-reference `structure.isotope.molecularWeight`.
R4 `structure.isotope.molecularWeight.amount` is 0..1 Quantity.
R6 `SubstanceDefinition.molecularWeight.amount` is 1..1 Quantity and `structure.molecularWeight` content-references it.
R4 has `structure.isotope`; R6 extracted element list has no `SubstanceDefinition.structure.isotope`.
freshReview.fmmEffect: Low FMM tempers assumptions about prevalence, but isotope and molecular-weight data can be substance-identity and radiopharmaceutical/regulatory content. The expert-dependent and potentially lossy migration keeps this in Revisit territory.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: R4 molecular-weight entries without `amount` fail R6 cardinality, and R4 isotope children are not accepted by the R6 structure.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: A less-breaking base design could keep `amount` optional in the base resource while adding warning/profile guidance for complete records, and retain `structure.isotope` as deprecated optional content. This weakens the R6 guarantee that a molecular weight has an amount and preserves legacy complexity, but it avoids forcing dummy data or isotope loss.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree with the existing concern that this break is not clearly justified; partially agree on impact because FMM0 reduces broad stability pressure even though the affected records can be high value.

findings.title: Substance status became a modifier with publication-status binding semantics

oldState.summary: R4 status was an optional CodeableConcept summary element, not marked as a modifier, with no binding in the base element.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 described status as `Status of substance within the catalogue e.g. approved` and did not require modifier processing for the element.

newState.summary: R6 status remains optional CodeableConcept but is marked `isModifier=true` and has a preferred binding to publication-status.

binding.description: The lifecycle status of an artifact.

flags.isModifierReason: This element is labelled as a modifier because it is a status element that can indicate that a record should not be treated as valid

newState.narrativeMd: R6 says status can be active or retired and explicitly marks it as a modifier because it can indicate that the record should not be treated as valid.

facts.newValue: status element can indicate that a record should not be treated as valid

impact.impactRationaleMd: The cardinality and type did not become stricter, so this is not an instance validation break by itself. It is a runtime/conformance break because R6 processors are expected to recognize the modifier semantics: a retired or invalid status can change whether the record should be used. Generated models and validators may also flag the element as modifier, affecting safety checks and data-access APIs.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Ignoring retired or invalid substance definitions can lead to use of obsolete or non-current catalogue entries.

justification.inferredGoal: Make lifecycle status safety semantics explicit to consumers.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Keep `status` non-modifier and rely on narrative guidance, preferred binding, or warning-level conformance guidance for retired records.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: This is not a hard instance validation break, but it is a real runtime/conformance change. The R6 goal of formally signaling that lifecycle status can affect safe use is reasonable, and a non-modifier alternative would be less disruptive but materially weaker.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: R6 could have retained the R4 non-modifier flag and documented that retired or inactive statuses require special handling. That base design would preserve older processor assumptions, but it would not give validators, generated models, or safety checks the explicit modifier signal that R6 uses for data that can change interpretation.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Avoids generated-code modifier churn but provides a weaker safety signal that implementations may ignore.

evidence.detail: R4 status is not a modifier and has no binding.
R6 status has preferred binding to `publication-status`.

examples.examplesMd: The R6 fragment is structurally representable as a CodeableConcept in R4, but R4 does not carry the same modifier flag semantics.

findings.narrativeMd: The status field now has formal modifier semantics. Systems that previously displayed or used a substance record without checking status must change behavior in R6, especially for retired or otherwise non-current definitions.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Existing coded status values are not rejected merely because of this flag, and the binding is preferred rather than required. The break is in processing obligations: R6 consumers cannot safely ignore a modifier element. R4-to-R6 migrations should update generated-code assumptions and modifier handling tests.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Update consumers to check `SubstanceDefinition.status` before using a definition. Ensure generated models expose the modifier flag and that validation pipelines treat status consistently with other modifier elements. Map local R4 status codes to the R6 publication-status value set when possible, but do not rely on preferred binding for hard validation.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The modifier flag is probably justified for lifecycle status. A backward-compatible alternative would have been narrative guidance only, but that would not give validators or generated code a formal signal.

freshReview.narrativeMd: `status` keeps the same basic shape but becomes a modifier and receives a preferred publication-status binding. This is not an old-valid/new-invalid instance break, but it is a real processing obligation for R6 clients and generated models: a retired or otherwise inactive definition may need different handling. The computable modifier signal is reasonable for lifecycle status.
keyEvidence: R4 `SubstanceSpecification.status` is 0..1 CodeableConcept and isModifier false.
R6 `SubstanceDefinition.status` is 0..1 CodeableConcept and isModifier true.
R6 status has preferred binding to `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/publication-status`.
R6 modifier reason says status can indicate that a record should not be treated as valid.
freshReview.fmmEffect: R4 FMM 0/trial-use lowers the compatibility burden, and the binding is preferred rather than required. The modifier change still matters for processors, but the safety rationale is proportionate.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: runtime/API/codegen: instances are not rejected solely by the flag change, but R6 processors and generated APIs must expose and respect modifier semantics.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: R6 could have kept `status` non-modifier and relied on prose or warnings. That would preserve older processing assumptions, but it would not give generic validators and clients a computable signal that lifecycle status can change safe use.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree: the runtime mechanism is real and the partial alternative is correctly identified, but the existing High runtime risk is stronger than the evidence supports for a FMM0 optional element.

findings.title: Name language gained a required all-languages terminology binding

oldState.summary: R4 name.language was an unbound `0..* CodeableConcept`.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 allowed implementers to populate name language with any CodeableConcept coding or text; the StructureDefinition did not attach a terminology binding.

newState.summary: R6 name.language is still `0..* CodeableConcept` but has a required binding to `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/all-languages|6.0.0-ballot4`.

binding.description: IETF language tag for a human language

terminologyComparison.terminologyNotesMd: No terminology expansion was performed. The impact assessment is based on binding strength and value set identity from the StructureDefinitions.

newState.narrativeMd: R6 requires codes to come from the all-languages value set, with a starter value set of `languages` also listed in the binding metadata.

impact.impactRationaleMd: The element remains optional, so instances that omit `name.language` are unaffected. But R4 instances that carry local or non-language codings can become invalid under the R6 required binding. This is a validation break for affected records and a codegen/runtime risk for enum-like language handling.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Incorrect language tagging can affect display, search, and multilingual regulatory labels, but is less likely to alter core substance identity.

justification.inferredGoal: Standardize name language tags using the common all-languages value set.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Use an extensible or preferred all-languages binding first, then tighten to required after legacy language codings can be mapped.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: Standardizing language tags is an interoperable and reasonable goal, and the element remains optional. The less-breaking alternative is real but materially weaker because R4 allowed arbitrary CodeableConcepts and a softer binding would continue to accept non-standard language identifiers.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: R6 could have introduced the all-languages value set with preferred or extensible strength, possibly with guidance to map legacy local language codes. That would preserve most populated R4 `name.language` instances, but it would not provide the same base conformance guarantee that language values are valid IETF language tags.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: Preserves local codings but weakens validation and reliable language-based processing.

evidence.detail: R6 binding strength is required and value set is `all-languages`.

examples.examplesMd: The coding system used by the all-languages expansion should be verified with terminology services; the example shows the intended need for standardized language tagging, not a certified code-system assertion.

findings.narrativeMd: `name.language` is a local terminology tightening. Existing R4 names that used site-specific CodeableConcepts for language now need standard language codes or risk R6 validation failure.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: Omitted language values remain valid. Populated values with non-conformant codings can be old-valid/new-invalid because R6 uses a required binding. Reverse conversion to R4 is structurally easy because R4 had no binding, but the R6 conformance guarantee is lost.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: Extract all `name.language` values and map them to standard language tags before R6 validation. Keep unmapped values in extensions or text only if local policy accepts that loss of codable conformance. Add terminology tests with valid tags, invalid local codes, and text-only CodeableConcepts.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change is interoperable but not fully backward-compatible. A preferred or extensible binding would have been less disruptive but less precise for multilingual processing.

freshReview.narrativeMd: `name.language` remains optional and repeatable, but R6 adds a required all-languages binding. R4 instances with local language codings can fail R6 terminology validation, while omitted language values are unaffected. Standardizing language tags is a reasonable interoperability goal, and this path is less central to substance identity than properties, relationships, or source material.
keyEvidence: R4 `SubstanceSpecification.name.language` is 0..* CodeableConcept with no binding in the StructureDefinition.
R6 `SubstanceDefinition.name.language` is 0..* CodeableConcept with required binding to `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/all-languages|6.0.0-ballot4`.
No terminology expansion comparison was performed; judgment is based on binding strength and value set identity.
freshReview.fmmEffect: R4 FMM 0/trial-use softens concern, and the element is optional. The required binding can still break populated local-code records, but the interoperability benefit is clear and the safety/business risk is limited.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: old-valid/new-invalid: populated R4 language CodeableConcepts outside the required R6 value set can fail validation; instances without `name.language` are unaffected.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: A preferred or extensible binding would be less disruptive and could ease legacy-code migration, but it would not give R6 the same base guarantee that language values are valid language tags.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree with the potential hard-break finding; the existing Medium impact is plausible for affected data, but low FMM and optionality keep the break probably acceptable.

findings.title: R6 adds substantial optional content that is not directly representable in R4 SubstanceSpecification

affectedLocation.newPath: SubstanceDefinition.version | classification | grade | note | manufacturer | supplier | characterization | moiety.measurementType | structure.technique | structure.representation.format | sourceMaterial.*

oldState.summary: R4 SubstanceSpecification lacks these R6 elements or carries only narrower older forms.
oldState.narrativeMd: R4 has no direct base elements for business version, manufacturer, supplier, characterization, grade, or the R6 representation/source-material refinements. Some concepts might fit extensions or separate companion resources, but not core `SubstanceSpecification` elements.

newState.summary: R6 SubstanceDefinition adds multiple optional fields and generalized value choices.
newState.narrativeMd: R6 adds `version`, `classification`, `grade`, repeatable `note`, `manufacturer`, `supplier`, a new `characterization` backbone, `moiety.measurementType`, `structure.technique`, `structure.representation.format`, and an inline `sourceMaterial` backbone with required country binding on `countryOfOrigin`.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: These are elements present in the R6 `SubstanceDefinition` snapshot with no same-suffix R4 `SubstanceSpecification` element after accounting for the resource rename.

impact.impactRationaleMd: These optional additions do not make existing R4 instances invalid when migrating forward, but they do create reverse-conversion and round-trip risk. An R6 instance using manufacturer/supplier references, characterization files, detailed sourceMaterial, or new property value choices cannot be losslessly expressed in core R4 `SubstanceSpecification` without extensions, companion resources, or out-of-band data.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: Manufacturer, supplier, characterization, and source-material fields may be operationally or regulatorily significant. Dropping them during R6-to-R4 conversion can lose provenance or identity context.

justification.inferredGoal: Expand the R6 substance definition model with fields needed for richer substance characterization and catalog management.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: No less-breaking forward base design is needed because these are optional R6 additions, not R4-to-R6 invalidating changes.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The finding describes R6-only optional content and reverse-conversion risk. It does not identify a base R6 design choice that invalidates R4 instances moving forward, so `backwardCompatibleAlternativeAvailable` should not be `No` or `Yes`; the calibration is not applicable to a forward breaking-design alternative.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: For R6-to-R4 workflows, implementers may need standard or local R4 extensions, companion-resource mappings, or lossy conversion policy. Those are backport and migration mitigations rather than less-breaking R6 base designs. The optional additions themselves can coexist with all R4-valid forward-migrated instances.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: The tradeoff is richer R6 expressivity versus lossy R6-to-R4 down-conversion; R4 extensions would be mitigations, not base R6 alternatives.

evidence.detail: R6 adds these root-level optional elements.
R6 defines inline sourceMaterial children including type, genus, species, part, and countryOfOrigin.
R4 SubstanceSpecification has no direct matching elements for these additions.

examples.examplesMd: R4 could preserve this information only through extensions, separate resources, or implementation-specific side tables.

findings.narrativeMd: R6 `SubstanceDefinition` is more expressive than R4 `SubstanceSpecification`. This is not a forward validation break for old data, but it is a material round-trip risk: systems that must down-convert R6 to R4 need an extension strategy for new operational, characterization, and source-material data.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: R4 validators will reject these R6 element names if they are placed directly on `SubstanceSpecification`. R6 instances using only common elements can be down-mapped more easily; instances using the new elements are not core-R4-representable without loss.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: For R6-to-R4 flows, define a policy for each new element: drop with audit, preserve in extensions, map to R4 companion resources where appropriate, or block conversion. Include round-trip tests that prove whether data survives the down-map and up-map.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: Optional additions are appropriate in the forward direction. The compatibility gap is unavoidable unless the project publishes standard R4 extensions or conversion maps for the new fields.

freshReview.narrativeMd: The listed R6 fields are optional additions or broader R6 expressivity. They can create lossy R6-to-R4 down-conversion, but they do not invalidate R4 `SubstanceSpecification` instances moving forward. For a fresh R4-to-R6 break review, this is migration awareness rather than a base compatibility problem.
keyEvidence: R6 adds optional root elements including `version`, `classification`, `grade`, `note`, `manufacturer`, `supplier`, and `characterization`.
R6 adds optional nested content such as `moiety.measurementType`, `structure.technique`, `structure.representation.format`, and inline `sourceMaterial` children.
R4 SubstanceSpecification has no direct core elements for several of these R6 additions.
The R6 additions are optional in the extracted StructureDefinition metadata.
freshReview.fmmEffect: The R4 FMM 0/trial-use context does not create a reason to object to optional R6 additions. If anything, low maturity supports allowing the successor model to add needed substance-definition content.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: R6-to-R4 loss: down-converting an R6 instance that uses new optional fields may require extensions, companion resources, or data loss; forward R4-to-R6 compatibility is not materially harmed by the additions themselves.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: No less-breaking R6 base design is needed for optional forward additions. R4 backport extensions or conversion maps are useful mitigations for reverse exchange, but they are not reasons to avoid the R6 fields.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: partially agree that reverse conversion can be lossy; disagree that the finding should be treated as a meaningful R4-to-R6 breaking design issue.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: No local non-base invariants were found on either R4 `SubstanceSpecification` or R6 `SubstanceDefinition`. Root `dom-*` and inherited `ele-*` expression changes were treated as base-artifact scope, not local findings.
No local slicing discriminators or slice definitions were found in the compared StructureDefinitions.
No fixed value, pattern value, or default value constraints were identified on local elements.
No local minValue, maxValue, maxLength, or regex constraints were identified.
The local substance-detail elements remain broadly summary elements in both versions. Material flag change was the `status` modifier flag and is reported separately.
The same-named R6 artifact is absent and `SubstanceDefinition` is the clear local successor candidate, but no official rename ConceptMap was available.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Identifier cardinality widened from single to repeatable in the successor model
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: R4 allowed at most one identifier at these locations; R6 allows multiple. This does not invalidate R4 data when moving forward.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Reverse conversion must choose, merge, or extension-preserve multiple R6 identifiers.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Description type changed from string to markdown
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: Plain strings are valid markdown content, so typical R4 description text can be carried forward without semantic loss.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Generated code may expose a different primitive type name, and R6 descriptions may contain markdown formatting that older R4 renderers treat as plain text.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Free-text comment is replaced by repeatable Annotation note
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: A simple R4 comment can be represented as `note[0].text`, and R6 is more expressive because Annotation can carry author and time metadata.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: The element name and datatype changed, so raw instances still need transformation; reverse conversion from multiple notes may be lossy.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: High-level type appears to become repeatable classification
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The successor field is optional and repeatable, so an R4 type can usually be mapped into one classification value.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: The match is semantic rather than an official mapping; verify local code systems and whether more specific R6 classifications should be used.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: The successor StructureDefinition status is active rather than draft
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The status of the StructureDefinition artifact does not by itself change instance validity.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: It does signal that the R6 successor is positioned as a more mature active resource in the ballot package.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: Many CodeableConcept elements gained example or preferred bindings
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: Example and preferred bindings do not make non-member codes invalid in the same way a required binding does.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Terminology-aware applications may still use these bindings to drive UI pick lists, validation warnings, or analytics, so code-system mapping may be beneficial.

followUpDependencies.reasonMd: Inherited changes such as base `language` binding, base extension text, and root `dom-*` invariant expression updates apply across resources and are intentionally excluded from this local `SubstanceSpecification` report.
R4 `SubstanceSpecification` referenced these companion resources, but their payload-level migrations require separate artifact analyses. This report only records the local reference-element break.
A dedicated R6 `SubstanceDefinition` review should confirm intended mappings, especially for property, relationship, source material, and characterization fields.

followUpDependencies.nameOrUrl: SubstanceDefinition local value sets including all-languages, publication-status, substance-relationship-type, product-characteristic-codes
followUpDependencies.reasonMd: Terminology expansion comparison would improve confidence for required and preferred binding impacts.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: No official R4-to-R6 diff, ConceptMap, or StructureMap was available in the local package for `SubstanceSpecification` to `SubstanceDefinition`. Element mappings are therefore based on StructureDefinition names, definitions, and local package evidence.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: An HL7-published cross-version map or migration guide for the substance model would confirm intended renames, splits, and data-loss handling.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: Terminology value sets were compared by binding metadata only. No terminology server expansion or code-difference analysis was performed.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Expand the R4 and R6 value sets with a terminology service and compare removed, added, and changed codes.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: The analysis did not use narrative specification pages, ballot change notes, or Jira tickets. Rationale and backward-compatibility judgments are inferred from computable definitions.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Review the R6 ballot narrative pages and change proposals for the substance model.
